title: How Electricity Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how electricity works, starting from the Big Bang and energy conservation, then covering the history of static electricity (Thales, William Gilbert, Ben Franklin, Coulomb, J.J. Thomson and the electron, Michael Faraday), atoms and conductors versus insulators, generators and turbines at Niagara Falls, voltage, current, resistance and power, circuits and loads, electric motors, grounding, transformers, the Tesla versus Edison AC/DC rivalry, and how electricity bills are calculated. The episode closes with a listener mail shout-out for Molly's birthday.

segments.title: Opening banter and social media
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter about Chuck's hat, Schoolhouse Rock and Electric Company theme songs, and plug the show's Twitter, Facebook and website.

segments.title: Energy, the Big Bang and electricity as a carrier
segments.summary: Josh explains that energy is conserved since the Big Bang and changes form, and that electricity is a secondary energy source that carries energy from one point to another to do work.

segments.title: Early static electricity experiments
segments.summary: The hosts describe Thales of Miletus rubbing amber with fur, the Greek origin of the word electricity, and William Gilbert coining the term. They distinguish static from current electricity and note early scientists thought electricity was a fluid.

segments.title: Franklin, Coulomb's law and the discovery of the electron
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Ben Franklin's positive and negative charge idea and the disputed kite experiment, Coulomb's law of charge attraction, the Leyden jar, and J.J. Thomson's discovery of a particle smaller than the atom, which he called a corpuscle and was later renamed the electron.

segments.title: Atoms, conductors and insulators
segments.summary: Atoms are described as protons, neutrons and orbiting electrons, with a neutral atom having equal protons and electrons. Materials are conductors when electrons are loosely bound (metal) and insulators when tightly bound (wood).

segments.title: Static electricity and generating current with magnets
segments.summary: Chuck explains static electricity using the balloon-on-sweater example and the doorknob shock. They then explain that moving magnets near conductive coils knocks electrons loose, producing current, building on Faraday's work.

segments.title: Hydroelectric power at Niagara Falls and power plants
segments.summary: George Westinghouse set up a hydroelectric plant at Niagara Falls in 1895 that used falling water to spin a turbine connected to a shaft and coils in magnets. Dams like Hoover Dam work similarly, and thermal plants use heat from coal or nuclear reactions to make steam that turns turbines.

segments.title: Voltage, current, resistance and power
segments.summary: Using a water-pipe analogy, the hosts explain voltage as electromotive force, current in amps, resistance in ohms, and power in watts as voltage times current. They note that 120 volts is the US household standard and that higher voltage means more danger.

segments.title: Circuits, loads, motors and grounding
segments.summary: A circuit is a closed loop, and a load such as a light bulb, battery or heater uses the electron flow. An electric motor converts electricity into mechanical energy. Grounding wires and prongs send residual charge into the earth for safety, as do lightning rods.

segments.title: Transformers, AC vs DC and the Tesla-Edison rivalry
segments.summary: Transformers step up voltage for long-distance transmission to reduce loss and step it down for homes. The hosts contrast DC batteries with AC current that alternates 60 times per second in the US and 50 in Europe, and recount the Tesla versus Edison war of the currents, with Westinghouse also mentioned.

segments.title: Calculating an electricity bill and kilowatt-hours
segments.summary: Using a space heater example at 10 amps and 120 volts, the hosts calculate 1,200 watts and 1.2 kilowatt-hours per hour, and explain that a dime per kilowatt-hour makes it 12 cents an hour. They advise checking appliance kWh tags.

segments.title: Rubber shoes and closing remarks
segments.summary: Josh wraps up the electricity topic, saying rubber is an insulator and pointing listeners to the HowStuffWorks search bar and kids science sites for more.

segments.title: Listener mail: Molly's birthday shout-out
segments.summary: Pearl writes that she and her best friend Molly listen to the show together and asks for a birthday shout-out for Molly, who turns 26 on April 9. The hosts wish her a happy birthday.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives contact details for Twitter, Facebook, email and the website and signs off.
